units.rationale: Source reading plus construction in a scratch copy supports fixing one attributed responsibility for this Candidate. installSnapshot installs the remote snapshot, sets lastApplied/lastSnapshot and, for a monotonic LogStore, calls removeOldLogs which deletes every log entry, but it never updates the cached last log identity; the sibling leader-side restoreUserSnapshot does call setLastLog for exactly this reason, and the MonotonicLogStore contract states the reset is required when gaps are not allowed. The composed requirement is that after a snapshot install the node's reported and compared last log entry must be re-derived (or the cache updated) so the follower can accept the leader's post-install AppendEntries. The claim is bounded to that recovery path with a monotonic store, excludes the non-monotonic path and the at-or-below-snapshot case, and is offered as ready_for_check; construction showed the emptied store with a cached index of 5 and snapshot index 2 rejecting the follow-up AppendEntries, but formal evidence requires the trusted runner.

audit_question.question: When a follower with a monotonic LogStore installs a remote snapshot whose index is below the follower's cached last log index, installSnapshot empties the log store (removeOldLogs) and sets lastSnapshot but never updates the cached last log identity; does the follower then report and compare a last log entry that no longer exists, so that it rejects every subsequent AppendEntries and keeps looping on snapshots instead of catching up - or does some other mechanism re-derive the identity?
audit_question.importance: A follower that cannot accept AppendEntries after a snapshot install cannot resynchronize: its cached last log index/term feed AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog, the RequestVote up-to-date comparison and the PrevLog decision inside appendEntries, so a divergence can keep the node permanently behind, withholding its participation in quorum and (for enough stuck voters) costing availability. The entries involved are uncommitted, so the concern is bounded liveness and recovery, not consensus safety or data loss.
contexts: Follower main goroutine handling an InstallSnapshot RPC while its cached last log index is above the incoming snapshot index
Injected LogStore that implements MonotonicLogStore with IsMonotonic() true, so the install path calls removeOldLogs instead of compactLogs
A leader that, after a successful install, sets the follower's nextIndex to snapshotIndex+1 and sends AppendEntries from there
event_paths: InstallSnapshot -> version/term checks -> snapshot sink created, copied and closed -> fsmMutateCh restore -> setLastApplied/setLastSnapshot -> removeOldLogs deletes all log entries -> lastLogIndex/lastLogTerm unchanged
leader sendLatestSnapshot success -> atomic.StoreUint64(&s.nextIndex, meta.Index+1) and commitment.match(peer.ID, meta.Index)
next AppendEntries with PrevLogEntry=meta.Index -> r.getLastEntry() uses the stale cached index above the snapshot index -> PrevLogTerm mismatch -> reject
later AppendEntries entries at indexes <= stale cached index -> r.getLastLog() used for classification -> r.logs.GetLog returns ErrLogNotFound on the emptied store -> reject
leader consumes resp.LastLog (getLastIndex = stale cache) -> s.nextIndex decremented until the leader's own log no longer covers it -> sendLatestSnapshot again

supporting_behavior_ids.B-snapshot-install: Cause/context: installSnapshot installs the snapshot, sets lastSnapshot/lastApplied and, for a monotonic LogStore, removes all log entries without updating the cached last log identity - the mechanism that can separate the cache from the store.

counterevidence: For a non-monotonic LogStore the install path calls compactLogs(req.LastLogIndex), which retains trailing entries, so the cached last log index stays consistent with the store

When the follower's cached last log index is at or below the snapshot index, getLastEntry and getLastIndex take the maximum of the log and snapshot values, so the PrevLog identity matches and the entries block appends from the lower cached index
installSnapshot does set lastApplied and lastSnapshot to the incoming index, so getLastEntry/getLastIndex of an empty-log follower still reflect the snapshot
The leader sets nextIndex to snapshotIndex+1 after a successful install, so any subsequent successful StoreLogs on the follower calls setLastLog and repairs the cache
unknowns: Whether a follower's cached last log index can exceed the leader's chosen snapshot index in a legal history (for example a previous leader's uncommitted suffix), which is what makes the emptied store diverge from the cache
Whether the resulting PrevLog/GetLog rejections terminate through a snapshot resend plus successful store, or repeat indefinitely with the cache never updated
Whether the divergence is confined to monotonic LogStore implementations and how common those are among caller-supplied stores
audit_question.trigger_rationale: The install path contains two facts that are not obviously compatible: installSnapshot never calls setLastLog, while the sibling leader-side restore path does, and the monotonic-store branch deletes all logs rather than retaining trailing ones. The MonotonicLogStore contract itself says the store must support removing all logs after snapshot restore, so the emptied store is intended; whether the cached identity is then re-derived is what stays unstated. Because the index relationship between the follower's cache and the leader's snapshot is not fixed by the code, the case needs to be isolated and, if reachable, executed.

scope.description: The in-repository FileSnapshotStore with retention at least two, holding two snapshots whose last-entry terms and indexes are ordered in opposite directions, listed through List.
assumptions: Both snapshots are created through the public Create/Write/Close path and are retained, so List returns both.
The store is otherwise healthy: metadata readable and versions supported.
excluded: Other SnapshotStore implementations supplied by callers
The downstream effect in sendLatestSnapshot or startup restore, which remains a limit rather than part of this obligation
Snapshots whose terms and indexes are ordered in the same direction, where both comparator statements agree

parameters.implementation_comparator: snapMetaSlice.Less compares Term before Index under sort.Reverse

units.rationale: The two messages are separately sourced statements of the same ordering obligation and the implementation adds no guard between them, so the responsibility can be fixed without assuming that a violation occurs: the store must place the highest Index first. The claim is bounded to the listing call and to the in-repository store, excludes the consumer consequence and other implementations, and is offered as ready_for_check.

audit_question.question: Does SnapshotStore.List return snapshots in descending applied-index order as the interface states, so that the first entry is the snapshot with the highest Index - or does FileSnapshotStore's Term-before-Index comparison return a lower-index snapshot first when two retained snapshots are inversely ordered, so that the leader ships and a restarting node restores an older applied state than the store actually holds?
audit_question.importance: The first list element is the snapshot the leader opens in sendLatestSnapshot to bring a lagging follower up to date and the first one NewRaft's restoreSnapshot tries to load. Selecting a lower-index snapshot because its last-entry term is higher can ship an outdated snapshot or restore an older applied state, which for a local storage duty is a state-recovery concern rather than a consensus-safety claim; the interface wording fixes the required order regardless of the consequence.
contexts: FileSnapshotStore with retention >= 2 holding two snapshots whose (term, index) positions are inversely ordered
Leader replication goroutine running sendLatestSnapshot for a far-behind follower
Node startup running restoreSnapshot over the same store
event_paths: snapshot store Create(version,index,term,...) -> sink Close -> directory renamed into place with meta.json
r.snapshots.List() -> getSnapshots reads each meta.json, skips .tmp and unreadable entries, sorts with sort.Reverse(snapMetaSlice)
snapMetaSlice.Less compares Term first, then Index, so the reversed order puts the higher-term snapshot first even when its Index is lower
sendLatestSnapshot -> snapshots[0].ID -> r.snapshots.Open(snapID) -> InstallSnapshot to the follower
NewRaft -> restoreSnapshot -> tryRestoreSingleSnapshot for each listed snapshot until one succeeds -> setLastApplied(snapshot.Index)

supporting_behavior_ids.B-snapshot-install: Consumer/consequence: the leader's sendLatestSnapshot opens snapshots[0] to ship to a lagging follower and NewRaft's restoreSnapshot loads the first snapshot that succeeds, so the list order decides which snapshot is sent or restored and therefore which applied state the peer or the restarting node adopts.

counterevidence: Within a single log lineage, terms are non-decreasing with index, so snapshots taken from one node's own log are ordered consistently by both comparators
The SnapshotStore interface is caller-implementable, so only the in-repository FileSnapshotStore is bound by this comparator
List returns at most the retain count and skips unreadable or unsupported snapshots, which limits how many entries can participate
unknowns: Whether a node can retain two snapshots whose positions are inversely ordered, for example a local snapshot with a high last-entry term next to a snapshot installed from a leader whose last entry has a lower term but a higher index
Whether selecting the lower-index snapshot in restoreSnapshot regresses applied state or makes the startup configuration scan fail on logs that were compacted up to the higher index
Whether the term-first comparator is deliberate authority ordering, in which case only the interface description is wrong
audit_question.trigger_rationale: The interface document and the comparator are two different statements of the same ordering obligation, and they disagree exactly when term order and index order are inverted across two retained snapshots - a situation the code neither prevents nor checks. Because the disagreement depends on a data configuration (which snapshots the store retains) rather than on a single call path, the obligation must be fixed and the comparison tested with snapshots created in the inverted order.

scope.description: A fresh store (no current term, log entry or snapshot) on which BootstrapCluster runs with a caller-supplied LogStore whose StoreLog fails once, followed by a retry on the same store.
assumptions: The server config and the initial configuration pass their validations.
The LogStore implements the interface faithfully, so StoreLog may return an error while the StableStore write has already succeeded.
excluded: Stores that cannot fail the log call
The RecoverCluster operator path, which remains an available remedy rather than part of this obligation
Any cluster-wide consequence; the duty is local to the store and the bootstrap guard

units.rationale: The ordering between the two durable writes and the guard that reads the first of them are both sourced, so the responsibility can be fixed without assuming the failure occurs: a store that cannot be seeded must not be reported as already bootstrapped. The claim is bounded to the bootstrap path with a failing StoreLog, excludes the operator recovery path and other store calls, and is offered as ready_for_check.

audit_question.question: When BootstrapCluster fails after writing the current term but before storing the bootstrap configuration entry, does the server remain bootstrappable - does a subsequent BootstrapCluster attempt still seed the store - or does HasExistingState's current-term check make the store look already bootstrapped so every retry returns ErrCantBootstrap while no configuration entry exists?
audit_question.importance: BootstrapCluster is the supported way to seed a brand-new server's storage. A partially completed bootstrap that permanently blocks retries would leave the server unable to form or join a cluster without operator intervention through a different recovery path, so the consequence is bounded availability and recovery rather than consensus safety.
contexts: Caller invoking BootstrapCluster on a store that HasExistingState reports as clean
Injected LogStore whose StoreLog call fails once after the stable current-term write succeeded
A later bootstrap attempt or NewRaft start reading the same store

BootstrapCluster -> logs.StoreLog(configuration entry at index 1) fails -> error returned to the caller
later BootstrapCluster -> HasExistingState reads keyCurrentTerm = 1 -> reports existing state -> ErrCantBootstrap before any log check
NewRaft on the same store -> setCurrentTerm(1) and lastLogIndex 0 -> follower with an empty configuration

supporting_behavior_ids.B-term-vote-persist: Context: this Behavior writes the same StableStore current-term key on the normal term-transition path, so the bootstrap write is a second establishment path for the same fact and the value alone cannot distinguish a bootstrapped server from one whose log write failed.

counterevidence: The failure requires the injected LogStore to return an error from StoreLog, which is outside the library's own control and does not occur for a healthy store
RecoverCluster exists as an operator path that can force a configuration onto such a store, so the state is not necessarily unrecoverable
HasExistingState also treats a non-empty log or snapshot as existing state, so a store that had genuinely been bootstrapped is still detected through those checks
unknowns: Whether an in-repository or caller-supplied LogStore returns an error from StoreLog after the stable write succeeded, i.e. whether the partial bootstrap is reachable rather than merely expressible
Whether every retry is rejected as already bootstrapped, or whether some later path re-derives the configuration
Whether RecoverCluster is the intended and sufficient operator remedy, which would bound the consequence to an explicit recovery step
audit_question.trigger_rationale: The two durable writes run in a fixed order with no rollback, and the key the first write sets is exactly what the bootstrap guard reads. The guard's own comment says a further attempt's error can be safely ignored, which presumes the state really is bootstrapped; whether a store failure can split the two writes and what the guard then reports is what must be tested.

scope.description: A node starting with an empty log and stable store and a FileSnapshotStore retaining two snapshots whose terms and indexes are ordered in opposite directions, so the restore path must choose between them.
assumptions: Both snapshots are readable and load successfully, so the choice is decided by the order alone.
The node has no log or stable state that could pin its applied baseline independently.
excluded: The leader's snapshot send path, which is a different consumer of the same order
The later configuration-scan behaviour when a hole lies above the adopted snapshot
Snapshot stores supplied by callers that do not implement this ordering

units.rationale: Recorded as a new sourced question anchored on the same principal Fact from its consumption side: the ordering fact is what the startup recovery selects by, and the recovery duty is that the adopted baseline must be the most advanced retained state. The claim is bounded to the in-repository store and the constructed retention, excludes the leader's send path and the later scan consequence, and is offered as ready_for_check.

audit_question.question: When a node restarts with an empty log and a snapshot store retaining two snapshots whose (term, index) positions are inversely ordered, does startup recovery adopt the snapshot with the highest applied index - the state the store actually holds most recently - or does it adopt the lower-index snapshot because the first listed entry is chosen by term order, leaving the node's applied baseline below what the store holds?
audit_question.importance: Startup recovery sets the node's applied baseline, which decides which entries are replayed and which state the FSM is restored to. Adopting a lower-index snapshot regresses the node's state relative to its own store until a leader re-supplies the missing range, so the concern is a recovery/state-selection duty; the same order also decides which snapshot a leader ships to a lagging follower.
contexts: Node startup with an empty log and stable store and a FileSnapshotStore retaining an inversely ordered pair
Recovery attempting the listed snapshots in order
Later replication that must re-supply entries above the adopted baseline if it is too low

NewRaft configuration scan from the adopted index to the last log index
leader appendEntries/snapshot install re-supplies entries above the adopted baseline

supporting_behavior_ids.B-snapshot-install: Context: the other consumer of the same ordering is the leader's sendLatestSnapshot, which also selects the first listed snapshot to ship to a lagging follower; the two consumers share the ordering duty.

counterevidence: restoreSnapshot falls through to the next listed snapshot when one fails to load, so a bad first choice does not necessarily prevent startup
A conformant store would list the highest index first and the recovery would adopt it, so the duty is met whenever the store honours the interface
Snapshots taken from one node's own log have terms and indexes ordered together, so the divergence requires the inverse pair rather than ordinary retention
The adopted snapshot is the node's own store content either way, so no state outside the node is discarded by the choice itself
unknowns: Whether a node can retain an inversely ordered pair in a legal history, for example an older local snapshot with a high last-entry term beside a snapshot installed from a leader whose last entry has a lower term but a higher index
Whether the startup configuration scan would then panic on a hole above the adopted baseline, which is a separate consequence not part of this duty
Whether callers expect recovery to prefer the highest applied index or the highest-term snapshot, which would decide whether the interface comment or the comparator is the normative statement
audit_question.trigger_rationale: The recovery path trusts the store's documented ordering and takes the first entry that loads, while the in-repository comparator orders by term first. The two statements only diverge for inversely ordered retention, a store state the code neither prevents nor checks, so the selection has to be observed with such a pair rather than assumed from the comparator alone.

First product of a fresh run: a sourced partial map of hashicorp/raft that establishes both core relationships and their connection. Formation/advancement (A1) is traced from Apply/ApplyLog through leader dispatchLogs, follower appendEntries, commitment.match/recalculate and processLogs application. Context/authority (A2) is traced through StableStore-backed term/vote persistence, the candidate election path, higher-term step-down and the leader lease. The connection is the commitment startIndex gate (a leader may only advance the commit index once a quorum has stored the first entry of its own term) together with the voter-set basis for quorum and the ErrLeadershipLost cleanup of inflight futures on step down. The core_overview is usable; the leadership-transfer handshake, the pipelined append path, user snapshot restore and startup reconstruction remain explicit open details and sourced surfaces rather than claimed coverage.

formation.explanation: A client command enters the leader's applyCh (B-apply-api) and is dispatched by the leader main loop (B-leader-dispatch), which assigns (Index,Term), stores it in the local LogStore, marks its own matchIndex and notifies replicators. Followers accept entries through AppendEntries only after the PrevLog identity matches and truncate conflicting suffixes (B-follower-append). Whenever any server reports that it has stored up to an index, commitment.match/recalculate raises commitIndex to the quorum median once it is at or beyond the leader's startIndex (B-quorum-commit, B-commit-term-rule). The leader then applies committed entries in index order to the FSM and resolves client futures (B-leader-apply).

context.explanation: Authority is a per-term value. Each node persists its current term and any vote through StableStore before acting (B-term-vote-persist). A follower whose heartbeat timer expires starts a candidate campaign, soliciting votes or pre-votes from voters of the latest configuration and winning at quorumSize (B-election); the winner's leadership is the context in which log dispatch is legal. Context is lost whenever a higher term is observed in any RPC or replication response (B-authority-loss) or when the leader fails its lease check (B-leader-lease); both transitions clear the known leader and invalidate the previous term's leadership.

connection.explanation: The two core lines meet at the startIndex rule and at the voter set. A leader may only advance commitIndex once a quorum of the current configuration has stored the first entry of the leader's term (B-commit-term-rule over B-quorum-commit), so formation is gated by current-term authority. Conversely, authority is defined over the voter configuration (B-election, B-config-eligibility), and losing authority (B-authority-loss) aborts pending formation work: runLeader's deferred cleanup answers inflight futures with ErrLeadershipLost while the durable log prefix and the already-applied FSM state remain. Established decisions from earlier terms persist as log entries but cannot be committed by a new leader until its own term entry is quorum-matched.

selections.rationale: First Candidate on the accepted v1 map, selected from the A1/A2 connection. The commit index is advanced by the commitment object (F-committed, established by B-quorum-commit/B-commit-term-rule) while client futures are completed by the leader main goroutine's inflight handling (B-leader-apply). The two are linked only through a capacity-1 commitCh and runLeader's deferred cleanup, so the ordering at an authority transition is not evident from the data structures alone. This question isolates whether every index counted as committed is consumed (applied in order, or later delivered from the durable log) and whether a future can be answered ErrLeadershipLost for an entry already counted committed. It is a lifecycle/consumption question for one principal Fact with a sourced A1 relationship and A2 context support; no violation is presumed.

Source reading answers this Candidate's specific suspicion, so the question is disposed as explained by existing mechanisms rather than escalated. The leaderLoop commitCh case reads commitment.getCommitIndex(), calls setCommitIndex and runs processLogs synchronously on the same goroutine, so a consumed notification cannot skip or reorder entries; if a higher-term RPC is selected before the notification is consumed, runLeader's deferred cleanup answers the still-inflight futures with ErrLeadershipLost and the entries remain durable. The public Apply contract explicitly documents that case as indeterminate ('There is no way to guarantee whether the write succeeded or failed'), and the node applies the committed index later from its durable log via the new leader's LeaderCommitIndex. No violation is presumed and no map change is proposed; the previously recorded edges and Behaviors still apply.

feedback.answered: Every index counted as committed by commitment.recalculate is either applied in order (processLogs walks idx from lastApplied+1 to index, taking each entry from the inflight futures map or the LogStore, and only then sets lastApplied) or, if the leader steps down before the commitCh notification is consumed, remains in the durable log and is applied on this node later when a leader supplies LeaderCommitIndex (follower appendEntries -> setCommitIndex(min(LeaderCommitIndex,lastIndex)) -> processLogs(idx,nil)). A future may indeed be answered ErrLeadershipLost for an entry the leader had already counted committed; that is the documented indeterminate outcome of the public Apply contract, not a mismatch between the reported outcome and the committed state, because ErrLeadershipLost does not assert non-commitment.
remaining: Independent execution corroborating the composed protection (a controlled schedule that triggers a step down in the window between the commitCh notification and its consumption) has not been performed; the conclusion here is a source-level explanation, not an execution witness.
feedback.rationale: The explanation rests on three independent sourced elements: (1) the single-goroutine serialization of the commitCh case versus the rpcCh/stepDown cases in leaderLoop; (2) runLeader's deferred cleanup that answers remaining inflight futures with ErrLeadershipLost while leaving the durable log untouched; and (3) the documented Apply contract in api.go that ErrLeadershipLost is indeterminate. Together these exclude the plausible alternatives 'a committed entry is silently skipped' and 'ErrLeadershipLost is reported as a definite failure'.

selections.rationale: New Candidate selected from an unread surface (Raft.restoreUserSnapshot, previously recorded as deferred) and from the same family of failure-path reasoning that produced the first finding, but for a genuinely different responsibility: the client-visible meaning of ErrAbortedByRestore versus when that error can actually be delivered. The public Apply contract states that ErrAbortedByRestore means 'the write effectively failed since its effects will not be present in the FSM after the restore', while restoreUserSnapshot answers every inflight logFuture with ErrAbortedByRestore before it creates and writes the replacement snapshot. If that snapshot creation or write then fails, the futures have already been told the write effectively failed even though no restore happened and the entries remain in the log. The question is scoped to the client/history boundary of F-committed and asks whether the abort can precede a failed restore, and whether those entries can still be committed and applied (making the reported outcome misleading). No defect is presumed: the configuration guard, the success path and the inflight bookkeeping are recorded as counterevidence.

Source reading supports fixing one attributed responsibility for this Candidate without presuming a violation. restoreUserSnapshot answers every inflight logFuture with ErrAbortedByRestore and removes it from leaderState.inflight before it calls r.snapshots.Create and writes/closes the replacement sink; the public Apply contract gives ErrAbortedByRestore the definite meaning that the write effectively failed and its effects will not be present after the restore. Two effects are therefore separated by a fallible call, so the composed requirement is that the abort signal must not be delivered unless the restore really completes or the still-logged entries can no longer be committed and applied. The claim is bounded to the leader's own restore handler with a caller-supplied SnapshotStore that fails after the abort, excludes the success path, the configuration-change guard and the quorum protocol, and is offered as ready_for_check for a later direct test.

New Candidate on the recovery responsibility (A3) that the map recorded as a deferred surface. The principal Fact is F-log-persisted, whose identity includes the server's cached last log index/term; the direct behavior is B-follower-append (the consumer that classifies incoming entries against that cache), with B-snapshot-install as the cause/context. Sourced observation: installSnapshot installs the remote snapshot and then, for a monotonic LogStore, calls removeOldLogs, which deletes every log entry; it updates lastSnapshotIndex/lastSnapshotTerm but never calls setLastLog, whereas the leader-side restoreUserSnapshot does call setLastLog for exactly this reason. For a monotonic store the log store can therefore be left empty while the cached last log index still names entries the store no longer holds, which is the same divergence class as the first confirmed finding but reached through a legal InstallSnapshot history rather than a store failure. This also corrects the earlier assumption that the snapshot path re-derives the reported identity. No defect is presumed: the non-monotonic path, the at-or-below-snapshot case and the post-install nextIndex are recorded as counterevidence.

Two newly read source ranges expose a discrepancy between the SnapshotStore interface contract and the in-repository FileSnapshotStore implementation, which is worth recording before an obligation or check is fixed. No defect is presumed and no map change is proposed: the new behavior/fact needed to hold this as a Candidate's principal coordinate will be added in the next related product once the discriminator is settled.

feedback.answered: The SnapshotStore interface documents that List returns snapshots in descending order with the highest index first (S-snapshot-list-contract), and FileSnapshotStore.List does compute its order through sort.Reverse(snapMetaSlice) over the metadata collected from each snapshot directory (S-file-snapshot-list). However snapMetaSlice.Less compares Term before Index, using Index only when the terms are equal (S-file-snapshot-sort). For two retained snapshots whose positions are inversely ordered - for example a local snapshot at (term 9, index 50) alongside one installed from a leader at (term 4, index 80) - the reversed order places the lower-index snapshot first, contradicting the documented 'highest index first' contract. Two consumers read that first element to choose state: the leader's sendLatestSnapshot opens snapshots[0] to ship to a lagging follower (S-replication), and NewRaft's restoreSnapshot restores the first snapshot that loads.
remaining: Whether a single node can in fact retain two snapshots whose (term, index) are inversely ordered, for example an older local snapshot with a higher last-entry term next to a newer snapshot installed from a leader whose last entry carries a lower term.

Whether selecting the lower-index snapshot in restoreSnapshot regresses applied state or makes the startup configuration scan fail on missing logs, and whether sendLatestSnapshot consequently ships an outdated snapshot to a lagging follower.
Whether the ordering is intended as term-first authority ordering rather than index recency, in which case the interface comment and the implementation disagree only in wording.
feedback.rationale: This is a contract-versus-implementation discrepancy read directly from two files, not an inference from names: the doc comment states the ordering obligation and the comparator states a different one. formation.explanation: A client command enters the leader's applyCh (B-apply-api) and is dispatched by the leader main loop (B-leader-dispatch), which assigns (Index,Term), stores it in the local LogStore, marks its own matchIndex and notifies replicators. Followers accept entries through AppendEntries only after the PrevLog identity matches and truncate conflicting suffixes (B-follower-append). Whenever any server reports that it has stored up to an index, commitment.match/recalculate raises commitIndex to the quorum median once it is at or beyond the leader's startIndex (B-quorum-commit, B-commit-term-rule). The leader then applies committed entries in index order to the FSM and resolves client futures (B-leader-apply).

context.explanation: Authority is a per-term value. Each node persists its current term and any vote through StableStore before acting (B-term-vote-persist). A follower whose heartbeat timer expires starts a candidate campaign, soliciting votes or pre-votes from voters of the latest configuration and winning at quorumSize (B-election); the winner's leadership is the context in which log dispatch is legal. Context is lost whenever a higher term is observed in any RPC or replication response (B-authority-loss) or when the leader fails its lease check (B-leader-lease); both transitions clear the known leader and invalidate the previous term's leadership.

connection.explanation: The two core lines meet at the startIndex rule and at the voter set. A leader may only advance commitIndex once a quorum of the current configuration has stored the first entry of the leader's term (B-commit-term-rule over B-quorum-commit), so formation is gated by current-term authority. Conversely, authority is defined over the voter configuration (B-election, B-config-eligibility), and losing authority (B-authority-loss) aborts pending formation work: runLeader's deferred cleanup answers inflight futures with ErrLeadershipLost while the durable log prefix and the already-applied FSM state remain. Established decisions from earlier terms persist as log entries but cannot be committed by a new leader until its own term entry is quorum-matched.

selections.rationale: Closing another unread peripheral area with a sourced explanation: the network transport's RPC admission and its heartbeat fast-path. The transport decodes each command, classifies strictly entry-less AppendEntries as heartbeats, and either calls the registered heartbeat handler directly on the connection goroutine or dispatches the RPC to the main consumer. The NewRaft comment requires that fast path to be safe when called concurrently with a blocking RPC, so the question is what the fast-path handler actually touches; reading it shows only atomic state writes, the leader lock and the last-contact lock, which is what makes the concurrent call safe. No discrepancy was found and no map object changes.

feedback.answered: The heartbeat fast path is safe as documented, and the transport's RPC admission adds no separate obligation. In the transport, each command is decoded, an InstallSnapshot reader is bounded by io.LimitReader(r, req.Size), and an AppendEntries command is treated as a heartbeat only under a strict conjunction - non-zero term, a leader address, PrevLogEntry and PrevLogTerm zero, no entries and LeaderCommitIndex zero - so an entry-carrying or commit-carrying AppendEntries always goes to the main consumer. When the fast path applies and a handler is registered, the handler is invoked directly on the connection goroutine; reading processHeartbeat and the appendEntries path it reaches shows that for such an entry-less heartbeat the handler can only call setState/setCurrentTerm (atomic stores), setLeader (which takes leaderLock and publishes an observation only on change), the previous-log check (skipped because PrevLogEntry is zero), the entries block (skipped because there are no entries), the commit update (skipped because LeaderCommitIndex is zero) and setLastContact (lastContactLock), and it reads the cached last index for the response under the state lock. No plain configurations field is written and no LogStore call is made on that path, so calling it concurrently with a blocking RPC does not race the main loop's configuration or storage mutations. The heartbeat classification is therefore load-bearing: it is what keeps the fast path free of the state the main thread owns.

feedback.answered: The ordering defect has two sourced consequences at startup, and they are consequences of the confirmed defect rather than separate obligations. First, restoreSnapshot tries the snapshots in List order and keeps the first that loads, setting lastApplied and lastSnapshot from it, so an inversely ordered retained pair makes the node adopt the lower-index snapshot: the applied state regresses relative to the newer snapshot the store holds until a leader re-supplies the missing range. Second, the configuration scan that follows in NewRaft starts at that restored snapshot index and walks up to the last log index calling GetLog for every index, panicking on a missing one; a hole in that range is exactly what a previous user restore leaves behind (that path burns the index above the last log and appends only above it), so restoring an older snapshot whose index sits below such a hole turns the ordering defect into a startup panic rather than a recoverable regression. The lower-index choice is what enables both outcomes: with the contract-conformant ordering the higher snapshot index would cover the hole.
remaining: Whether a node can legally hold the two ingredients together: a retained pair whose (term, index) are inversely ordered and a burned-index hole above the lower snapshot but below the higher one. The ordering half is confirmed; the coexistence with a user-restore hole is not.

formation.explanation: A client command enters the leader's applyCh (B-apply-api) and is dispatched by the leader main loop (B-leader-dispatch), which assigns (Index,Term), stores it in the local LogStore, marks its own matchIndex and notifies replicators. Followers accept entries through AppendEntries only after the PrevLog identity matches and truncate conflicting suffixes (B-follower-append). Whenever any server reports that it has stored up to an index, commitment.match/recalculate raises commitIndex to the quorum median once it is at or beyond the leader's startIndex (B-quorum-commit, B-commit-term-rule). The leader then applies committed entries in index order to the FSM and resolves client futures (B-leader-apply).

context.explanation: Authority is a per-term value. Each node persists its current term and any vote through StableStore before acting (B-term-vote-persist). A follower whose heartbeat timer expires starts a candidate campaign, soliciting votes or pre-votes from voters of the latest configuration and winning at quorumSize (B-election); the winner's leadership is the context in which log dispatch is legal. Context is lost whenever a higher term is observed in any RPC or replication response (B-authority-loss) or when the leader fails its lease check (B-leader-lease); both transitions clear the known leader and invalidate the previous term's leadership.

connection.explanation: The two core lines meet at the startIndex rule and at the voter set. A leader may only advance commitIndex once a quorum of the current configuration has stored the first entry of the leader's term (B-commit-term-rule over B-quorum-commit), so formation is gated by current-term authority. Conversely, authority is defined over the voter configuration (B-election, B-config-eligibility), and losing authority (B-authority-loss) aborts pending formation work: runLeader's deferred cleanup answers inflight futures with ErrLeadershipLost while the durable log prefix and the already-applied FSM state remain. Established decisions from earlier terms persist as log entries but cannot be committed by a new leader until its own term entry is quorum-matched.

selections.rationale: Closing two more residual items with sourced readings: the FSM apply paths that turn a committed index into an applied batch, and the network pipeline that pairs requests with responses. Both were listed as unread or only partially read, and both are relevant because the first decides when a barrier future resolves relative to the entries around it and the second decides whether an acknowledgement can be attributed to the wrong request.

feedback.answered: Neither path adds a contract discrepancy. In the FSM manager, a LogBarrier entry is delivered to the FSM goroutine (prepareLog returns a commit tuple for it) but is never sent to the FSM itself: the batching path filters it out before ApplyBatch, and the single-entry path has no barrier case, so in both cases its future is resolved after the batch containing it has been applied, which is what Barrier's contract asks for. A LogConfiguration entry with no ConfigurationStore is deliberately not counted in the single-entry path's internal index while the batching path does send LogConfiguration to ApplyBatch, and the FSM interface documents that ApplyBatch may receive LogConfiguration, so the two shapes differ in a way the interface states rather than contradict. In the network transport, the pipeline writes each request and then hands its future to a decoder that reads exactly one response per future in the same order on the single connection, with back-pressure instead of reordering, and raft's pipeline is driven by one replication goroutine per follower, so FIFO correspondence between requests and acknowledgements holds for this use.

feedback.answered: A client future created by Apply/ApplyLog does not receive the node's shutdown channel, so its Error() method can block forever rather than returning when the node stops. In the shared deferError, Error() selects only on the response channel or on d.ShutdownCh, and init() creates only the response channel; the three places that set ShutdownCh on a future are the user-restore future, the snapshot-install future and the snapshot request, so a logFuture from Apply has a nil ShutdownCh. The main run loop exits when shutdownCh closes without draining applyCh, and Shutdown closes shutdownCh and sets the state without responding to futures already enqueued. With the default unbuffered applyCh a send only succeeds when the loop receives the future, but Config.BatchApplyCh buffers the channel, so a future can be accepted while the loop is busy and then be abandoned when the node shuts down, leaving the caller blocked in Error() indefinitely.
remaining: Whether an Apply future can actually be pending at shutdown with BatchApplyCh enabled, which needs a running loop and a controlled schedule to observe.

feedback.answered: The Apply/ApplyLog future completion lead cannot be turned into a confirming check with the observation shape available here. The mechanism is read: a logFuture carries no shutdown channel, so Error() selects only on its response channel, and Shutdown closes shutdownCh without draining applyCh, so a future already accepted into the buffered channel is never answered. What a check could observe is that the future's Error() does not return within some window, and per the review criteria a finite window records non-completion rather than a deadline violation or indefinite stalling, so it can neither confirm nor bound the lead; and to make the pending state deterministic the harness would have to omit the running loop, which removes the very consumer whose behaviour is in question. A check that starts the loop instead would race the loop's own receipt of the future, so its outcome would not be a controlled schedule. Recording this as an explicit limitation of the lead rather than attempting the experiment keeps the run's evidence sound.
remaining: The Apply/ApplyLog shutdown-completion lead stays a deferred surface with its sources; it needs either a caller-visible contract fixing the required outcome or an observation mechanism that distinguishes a lost future from a slow one.

feedback.answered: The vote-withholding scenario is identified and ready to construct, using the same premise as the first confirmed append scenario. After a follower truncates its conflicting suffix and the following StoreLogs fails, its real log ends at the surviving prefix (index 1, term 1) while its cached last entry still reads (index 3, term 2). A RequestVote at the next term whose candidate log ends at (index 2, term 2) is strictly more up to date than the node's real log, so it must be granted; but the vote handler compares the candidate's LastLogTerm/LastLogIndex with r.getLastEntry(), which is served from the stale cache, so term equality with a smaller candidate index rejects the vote. The check's discriminator is therefore the handler's own Granted field: granted should be true and is expected false. This would move the claim's consequence from append rejection to vote withholding, which is the availability question the claim's unknowns leave open, and it needs the same injectable failing store and the same conflict drive as the accepted first scenario, plus a direct requestVote call on the same node.
remaining: Whether the withheld vote can change an election outcome in a legal cluster configuration, which is the cluster-level consequence beyond the local handler result.

items.rationale: Applicability: appendEntries is the follower entry point that classifies incoming entries against the cached last log identity, removes a conflicting suffix with r.logs.DeleteRange(entry.Index, lastLogIdx), and only then calls r.logs.StoreLogs and r.setLastLog on success (S-raft-appendentries). The LogStore interface declares StoreLogs and DeleteRange as independent error-returning operations (S-logstore), so a caller-supplied store that lets DeleteRange succeed and then fails StoreLogs is a legal object under the interface contract; the claim's premise therefore applies to this execution, and the unit scope explicitly fixes a Follower with a stored suffix and a faithfully failing store. Observation validity: the harness drives the real handler with a real RPC struct and no protocol modification; the prerequisite events conflict_suffix and store_logs_failed were matched with alias_indices {conflict:0, failure:1}, correlated by node n1 and the same truncated_to value, and the probe event's identity field node is shared with them, so the result belongs to the same operation rather than a neighbouring one. The assertion compares the handler's own Success field (accepted), which is exactly the duty: after the failure the node must not keep rejecting otherwise valid AppendEntries for the removed range. The measured witness at event index 3 is complete and applicable (accepted=false) while the trace also records the divergence (cached_index 3, stored_index 1, consistent false), so the comparison reflects the written obligation and not a scenario constant or an unobserved assumption. Cause and consequence are kept separate: this review confirms the in-scope comparison between the cached identity and the node's acceptance of replication; it does not by itself establish a cluster-wide effect or a safety violation. Unresolved conditions preserved as limitations are independent of this duty's applicability and of the observation's validity, so they do not block the correspondence judgment for this bounded scope.

items.rationale: Applicability: restoreUserSnapshot is the leader handler reached through Raft.Restore, and its only entry conditions are a supported snapshot version and a configuration whose committed index equals its latest index (S-raft-restoresnapshot, S-api-restore); the harness establishes both directly, so the obligation applies to this execution rather than to an unreachable branch. The SnapshotStore interface permits Create to return an error, so a faithful store failing that call is a legal caller-supplied object under the fixed scope, and no protocol behaviour is altered. Observation validity: the abort_delivered event records that restoreUserSnapshot returned an error and that the inflight future was answered with the handler's own ErrAbortedByRestore value ('snapshot restored while committing log'), which is the real signal the client sees rather than a constructed label (S-api-restore-contract). The abort_outcome event's identity field node is shared with the admitted prerequisite, so the result is correlated to the same operation. effects_absent is derived from two independent observed facts: the entry is still present when read back from the LogStore at its own index, and the commitment object's commit index has reached that index. Reading the commit decision from the commitment object is appropriate here because that object owns the commit index and no leader loop consumes commitCh in this controlled schedule; raftState.commitIndex staying at zero reflects the absent loop, not a different decision, and the review keeps that distinction explicit. Meaning: the assertion compares the documented outcome of ErrAbortedByRestore - the write's effects absent - against the observed state after a failed restore, so the witness bears on the written responsibility and not on an unrelated value. Observation validity: the config_entry_error event carries the handler's own returned error and Success=false, the error_path_identity event records the two independently read facts (cached_index 3 from raftState via getLastLog and stored_index 2 from the LogStore's LastIndex), and the result event's identity field node is shared with the admitted prerequisite, so the observation belongs to the same operation. The assertion compares the append handler's own Success field for the leader's next valid request, which is the duty the obligation states, rather than a derived proxy. Meaning: the request that is rejected is otherwise valid - its term equals the node's current term and its PrevLog entry equals the surviving stored prefix with the term that entry actually has - so the rejection follows from the stale cached index causing GetLog on the index DeleteRange removed; the identity event records that divergence separately from the compared acceptance value, keeping cause and proposition distinct. This scenario is the second independent path for the same requirement and does not replace the StoreLogs-failure scenario; both bear on the one obligation, and neither is asserted to be safety-relevant. Unresolved conditions preserved as limitations do not affect this duty's applicability or the validity of the measured comparison.
items.report_title: 追加条目配置解析失败路径的对应性审查
items.report_answer: 在协议版本 2 的跟随者上，冲突的弃用成员条目被成功写入后解析失败并提前返回，缓存最后索引仍为 3 而存储最后索引为 2，随后对该区间的合法 AppendEntries 被拒绝（accepted=false）；该比较在本义务范围内成立，真实领导者是否产生该条目仍待定。
limitations: The deprecated entry payload is artificially undecodable; the check does not establish that a real leader emits such an entry, and a protocol-version-3 cluster never uses the deprecated entry types.
Only one follower without the main loop is exercised; the confirmed comparison is local to the append handler, with no cluster-wide consequence claimed.
This is the second scenario for the same responsibility and does not by itself settle the StoreLogs-failure path or any other consumer of the cached identity beyond the append handler's acceptance.
Whether a production LogStore or peer payload actually produces this combination (store succeeds, configuration decode fails) is left open.

items.rationale: Applicability: the SnapshotStore interface states the required order and names the property to hold (highest index first), and FileSnapshotStore implements List for exactly that interface, so the obligation applies to this object. The harness creates both snapshots through the public Create/Write/Close path with a supported version, a real in-memory transport only to satisfy the signature, and a retention of two so that both remain; nothing in Create, getSnapshots or the comparator constrains the relationship between term and index, so a store holding (term 9, index 50) alongside (term 4, index 80) is a legal state rather than an artificial impossibility. Observation validity: the prerequisite snapshots_created recorded both_retained true and matched on the same label used as the result identity; the compared field highest_first is computed inside the harness from the returned metadata by comparing the first element's Index with the maximum Index across the returned elements, so max_index 80 comes from the store's own output rather than from a scenario constant, and the result event also records the two terms, which shows the inversion that explains the outcome. Meaning: the assertion compares the contract's ordering statement against the observed order; the check deliberately does not compare consumer behaviour, and the review does not extend the result to sendLatestSnapshot or startup restore, both of which remain excluded limits. The record also keeps the alternative explicit - if term-first ordering were the intended rule, the interface sentence would be the incorrect statement - and this check tests the written contract, so the confirmation is of the written requirement, not of a claim that the code is wrong in intent. Unresolved conditions preserved as limitations concern whether a running node ever retains inversely ordered snapshots and what the downstream effect would be; neither changes this duty's applicability nor the validity of the observation for the constructed retention.
items.report_title: 快照列表排序契约检查的对应性审查
items.report_answer: 在保留两个（term 与 index 反向排序）快照的真实 FileSnapshotStore 上，List() 返回的首个 index 为 50 而实际最大 index 为 80（highest_first=false），与接口所述“最高 index 在前”不符；该比较针对写入的接口契约成立，运行中是否会出现这种保留组合仍待定。
limitations: The inversely ordered pair is constructed directly through the public snapshot API; whether a running node retains such a pair (for example a local snapshot with a high last-entry term next to a snapshot installed from a leader whose last entry has a lower term but a higher index) is unestablished.
The consequence in sendLatestSnapshot and NewRaft.restoreSnapshot is excluded from the obligation; this check confirms the listing contract only, not a state-regression outcome.
Only the in-repository FileSnapshotStore is tested; other SnapshotStore implementations are caller-supplied and not bound by this comparator.

The check cannot settle whether the term-first comparator or the interface wording is the intended normative statement; it confirms that the written interface contract is not met for this configuration.

items.rationale: Applicability: BootstrapCluster is a public function whose LogStore and StableStore are caller-supplied, so a store that returns an error from StoreLog after the stable term write is a legal object under the interface contracts, and the harness starts from a clean store that HasExistingState confirms is empty, so the bootstrap path applies rather than being blocked before it runs. Observation validity: the bootstrap_attempt event records the first attempt's error and that the simulated store failure actually fired, and the bootstrap_outcome event records the guard's answer, the retry error text and the log index, all under the same storage label used as the identity field, so the result is correlated to the admitted operation rather than to a neighbour. The compared field retry_allowed is not a scenario constant: it is derived from the second attempt's own error being nil together with a positive observed log index, which distinguishes a genuinely seeded store from one that was merely accepted; the retained log_index_after_retry of zero shows that no configuration entry exists, so the guard's report of existing state cannot be attributed to a completed bootstrap. Meaning: the comparison bears on the written responsibility - a store that cannot be seeded must not be reported as already bootstrapped - and the review keeps it separate from the wider consequence, which is not asserted: the recovery is local, the entries involved are the bootstrap seed, and RecoverCluster remains an untested operator alternative. Unresolved conditions preserved as limitations concern whether production stores fail in this position and whether the operator remedy is intended, and neither changes this duty's applicability or the validity of the measured comparison for the simulated failure.
items.report_title: 引导写入部分失败后重试被阻止的对应性审查
items.report_answer: 在一次性 StoreLog 失败的干净存储上，BootstrapCluster 首次失败后 HasExistingState 报告为已有状态，随后的重试被拒绝（bootstrap only works on new clusters），日志索引仍为 0，即未写入任何引导配置条目；该比较在本恢复义务范围内成立，生产存储可达性与 RecoverCluster 补救仍待定。
limitations: Only one StoreLog failure is simulated on an in-memory store; whether an in-repository or production LogStore fails at that point is unestablished, so the premise is legal and expressible but not shown to arise from a specific shipped store.
The RecoverCluster operator path is excluded from the obligation and not exercised, so the check does not show that no recovery exists; it shows that the ordinary retry is blocked.
The check is local to the store and the bootstrap guard; no cluster-wide availability consequence is claimed.
Only the single-StoreLog failure point is instantiated; other store calls in the function are not separately exercised.

items.rationale: Applicability: restoreSnapshot lists the snapshots and keeps the first whose Open and FSM restore succeed, setting lastApplied and lastSnapshot from it, so with an empty log and stable store the adopted snapshot is the sole source of the node's applied baseline and the recovery path applies. The store is a real FileSnapshotStore retaining two readable snapshots, so the choice is decided by order rather than by a failed load, and an inversely ordered pair is a legal store state because Create accepts any index and term. Observation validity: the snapshots_prepared event carries the store's own metadata (retained, max_index, first_listed_index) and matched as the admitted prerequisite, and the startup_recovery event carries the node's adopted applied index, the adopted snapshot index and the same maximum under the shared node identity, so both sides of the comparison are sampled from the objects rather than from scenario constants. The compared field newest_adopted is an equality between the node's own applied index and the highest index the store holds, which is the duty as written; the retained snapshot_index of 50 shows the adoption, not merely a failure to start. Meaning: the check keeps to the recovery-selection responsibility and does not extend the result to the leader's send path or to the later configuration scan, which the obligation excludes; it confirms that recovery follows the list order, which the interface says is highest-index-first, and does not itself assert that the comparator is wrong in intent. Unresolved conditions preserved as limitations concern whether a running node retains such a pair and what the later scan would do, and neither changes this duty's applicability or the validity of the measured comparison for the constructed retention.
items.report_title: 启动恢复快照选择检查的对应性审查
items.report_answer: 在保留两个（term 与 index 反向排序）快照、日志与稳定存储为空的节点上，启动恢复采用了先列出的索引 50 快照，而存储中最高索引为 80（applied_index=50, newest_adopted=false），即恢复基线低于存储所持有的最新状态；该比较在本恢复义务范围内成立，运行中是否会出现这种保留组合仍待定。
limitations: The inversely ordered pair is constructed directly through the public snapshot API; whether a running node retains such a pair is unestablished.
Only the in-repository FileSnapshotStore is exercised; callers supplying other stores are not bound by this ordering.
The leader's snapshot send path and the later configuration-scan behaviour when a hole lies above the adopted snapshot are excluded from this obligation and not observed here.
The check shows the recovered baseline is below the newest retained state; it does not measure how long a cluster takes to re-supply the missing range.

items.rationale: Applicability: sendLatestSnapshot lists the store, opens the first entry and sends LastLogIndex/LastLogTerm taken from that snapshot's metadata, so the contract's ordering sentence directly governs what the leader puts on the wire for a lagging follower. The store is a real FileSnapshotStore retaining two readable snapshots, so the choice is decided by order rather than by a failed open, and an inversely ordered pair is a legal state because Create accepts any index and term. Observation validity: the snapshots_prepared event carries the store's own metadata and matched as the admitted prerequisite, and the snapshot_sent event carries the sent flag, the sent index and term and the store's maximum under the shared node identity, so the compared field newest_sent is an equality between the value the leader actually sent and the highest index the store holds rather than a scenario constant; sent being true rules out a send failure as the cause. The transport substitution does not weaken the comparison: the send path builds and passes the request the real RPC would carry, and only the delivery is intercepted, so the recorded metadata is the leader's own choice. Meaning: the result confirms the send-side consumer named by the claim and does not extend to the follower's install behaviour or to the recovery path, which was confirmed separately; the same ordering cause underlies both, and the review keeps the requirement, not the consumer, as the object judged. Unresolved conditions preserved as limitations concern whether a running node retains such a pair and the fact that no live follower was involved, and neither changes this duty's applicability or the validity of the measured comparison.
items.report_title: 领导者快照发送选择检查的对应性审查
items.report_answer: 在保留两个（term 与 index 反向排序）快照的领导者上，sendLatestSnapshot 实际发送的 LastLogIndex 为 50（term 9），而存储中最高索引为 80（sent=true, newest_sent=false），即向落后跟随者发送了较旧的快照；该比较在本排序义务范围内成立，运行中是否会出现这种保留组合仍待定。
limitations: The inversely ordered pair is constructed directly through the public snapshot API; whether a running node retains such a pair is unestablished.
The RPC delivery is intercepted by a transport wrapper, so the check observes the leader's selection rather than a live follower receiving the snapshot.
Only the in-repository FileSnapshotStore is exercised; other implementations are caller-supplied.
The check does not measure any consequence on the follower side, such as the installed snapshot index or the log reset that follows.

items.rationale: Applicability: the premise is the already-accepted scenario - a follower truncates its conflicting suffix with DeleteRange and the following StoreLogs fails - so the store retains only the surviving prefix while the cached last log identity still names the removed suffix; the LogStore interface permits that failure and the vote handler is a legal consumer of the same cached value, so the responsibility applies to this execution. The vote request itself is legal: it carries the node's current term, the configuration is empty so the membership and suffrage checks are skipped, no prior vote exists in this term, and the candidate's log position (index 2, term 2) is deliberately chosen to be strictly more up to date than the node's real log, which is what the up-to-date rule requires to be granted. Observation validity: the vote_precondition event records both identities read independently - cached_index and cached_term from raftState via getLastLog, and real_index and real_term from the LogStore's own LastIndex and the entry read back at that index - and it matched as the admitted prerequisite; the vote_decision event carries the handler's own Granted field together with the candidate position under the shared node identity, so the compared value is the decision under test. Meaning: the refusal isolates the cache as the cause, because the candidate is not less up to date than the real log and no other vote-path precondition differs; the review therefore reads the result as the vote-facing consequence of the same confirmed divergence and does not extend it to an election outcome, which remains an open limit. One harness labelling detail is noted for transparency: in the result event the field named real_term carries the error returned alongside LastIndex rather than the entry term, so it is null; the correct real term is carried by the precondition event (real_term 1), and the compared field granted and the identity field node are unaffected. Unresolved conditions preserved as limitations concern the artificial failure and the cluster-level consequence, and neither changes this duty's applicability or the validity of the measured comparison.
items.report_title: 截断失败后拒绝投票检查的对应性审查
items.report_answer: 在截断冲突后缀且 StoreLogs 失败后，缓存最后条目仍为 (index 3, term 2) 而真实日志止于 (index 1, term 1)；对日志为 (index 2, term 2) 的候选者（实际更新）投票被拒绝（granted=false），说明同一缓存偏差也会扣留选票；该比较在本义务范围内成立，集群级后果仍待定。
limitations: The stale cache is produced by a single artificially injected StoreLogs failure; whether a production or in-repository store fails at that point is unestablished.
The check observes the local vote decision, not an election outcome; whether the withheld vote can change a leadership change in a legal configuration is open.

In the result event the field named real_term is the LastIndex error placeholder rather than the entry term; the correct real term appears in the precondition event, and the field is not used by the comparison.
Only the cached-identity cause is exercised; term, configuration, suffrage and prior-vote conditions are held fixed.
